topics.title: 31.1 FIFO
topics.summary: First in, first out evicts the block that entered earliest among the eligible residents. Hits do not refresh its position. FIFO is simple because insertion age, rather than every access, determines replacement order. Insertion age can be a poor predictor of future use. A frequently accessed old block may be evicted while a newer block that will never be reused remains. FIFO also lacks the general stack property associated with exact LRU, so increasing capacity does not guarantee fewer misses for every trace.

topics.title: 31.2 LRU
topics.summary: Least recently used evicts the block whose most recent access is oldest. Hits refresh recency. It exploits the assumption that recently used blocks are more likely to be used again soon. Exact LRU requires tracking access order, which has a cost. Hardware often uses approximations or other policies. LRU can also perform poorly on cyclic scans slightly larger than capacity: every returning block may have just been evicted.

topics.title: 31.3 Optimal replacement
topics.summary: Optimal replacement evicts the block whose next use lies farthest in the future, or that will never be used again. With a fully known trace, it provides a lower bound on misses for the stated cache model. It is not generally implementable online because future accesses are unknown. Its purpose is comparison: it separates unavoidable misses under the model from misses caused by a practical policy’s limited information. Calling a policy “optimal” requires specifying the objective and assumptions.

topics.title: 31.4 Eviction
topics.summary: Eviction removes a resident block to make space or satisfy another policy. Its cost depends on the block’s state. A clean copy can often be discarded; a modified copy may require propagation before its only current contents are lost. Eviction can also disrupt future locality. A streaming workload may evict a small hot set and then immediately require that set again. Software techniques such as separating phases or limiting batch size can sometimes reduce this interference.

topics.title: 31.5 Dirty blocks
topics.summary: A dirty block contains modifications not yet reflected in the next level according to a write-back policy. Evicting it requires preserving those modifications through the appropriate writeback path. Dirty state therefore adds work beyond fetching the incoming block. Dirty does not mean corrupted. It means newer than the backing copy at the relevant level. The term applies similarly to file-cache pages whose updates have not yet been written according to the filesystem’s policy.

topics.title: 31.6 Clean blocks
topics.summary: A clean block matches the relevant backing copy under the cache’s protocol. It can be discarded without losing unique modifications. A later access may fetch it again if needed. Cleanliness and usefulness are different properties. A clean block may be extremely valuable to retain because it will be reused immediately, while a dirty block may never be referenced again. Replacement policy must balance future usefulness, writeback cost, and implementation constraints.
